Notorious for humiliating defendants and handing down frequent death sentences, this German judge presided over the People's Court from 1942 to 1945 — who is he?
Born in Paris to a family of Georgian political refugees, this career diplomat became the first woman ever elected president of her adopted country — who is she?

Touched off by the staged 1931 Mukden incident and the puppet state of Manchukuo, this 1937–1945 conflict — China's largest war of the 20th century — is often called the start of World War II in Asia. What was it?
Second Sino-Japanese War: 1937–1945 conflict in East Asia. It is often regarded as the beginning of World War II in Asia, as the wars became heavily intertwined after Japan's entry into World War II.

Known as 'The Destroyer' within the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Vishnu, this deity is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects, and transforms the universe in one major tradition. Who is this god?
Shiva: Major deity in Hinduism. Shiva is one of the five equivalent deities in Panchayatana puja of the Smarta tradition of Hinduism.
A Thracian gladiator born near the Strymon river, this figure led an escaped-slave uprising against the Roman Republic known as the Third Servile War — who was he?
Spartacus: Thracian gladiator who led a slave revolt. Spartacus is described to be born near the Strymon river, in Thrace (now known as Bulgaria), possibly from the Maedi tribe.
Sparked by Arab Spring protests against Bashar al-Assad in March 2011, this nearly 14-year conflict ended with the regime's fall in December 2024 — what is it?
Syrian civil war: 2011–2024 armed conflict in Syria.

Ruling the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy from 493 to 526 and later regent of the Visigoths too, this king received the old Western imperial regalia from Constantinople and was addressed by Italy's aristocracy as princeps. Who was he?
Theodoric the Great: King of Italy from 493 to 526. As ruler of the combined Gothic realms, Theodoric controlled an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea.

Breaking out in 1990 between Moldovan government forces and pro-separatist fighters backed by Russia's 14th Army, this conflict over a breakaway region ended with a ceasefire in July 1992 that still holds — which conflict?
Transnistrian War: 1990–1992 separatist conflict in Moldova. Cojocaru, the Moldovan defeat in this war directly led to implementation of Moldovan neutrality.

Sparked by a suppressed student demonstration in Prague on International Students' Day in November 1989, this peaceful transfer of power ended 41 years of one-party rule in Czechoslovakia — what was it called?
Velvet Revolution: Democratization process in Czechoslovakia in 1989.
This Chinese diplomat served as ambassador to Japan before becoming Minister of Foreign Affairs and later director of the Communist Party's Central Foreign Affairs Commission Office — who is he?
Raised in Liverpool as the half-nephew of a Nazi dictator, this man later fought against his own uncle's regime in the US Navy — who is he, after changing his name postwar?
William Stuart-Houston: Half-nephew of Adolf Hitler (1911–1987)
A Hindu monk who became Uttar Pradesh's longest-serving and first two-term chief minister, he won five straight terms from Gorakhpur after entering parliament at just 26 — who is he?
Yogi Adityanath: Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 2017.
Who wrote Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

Universal Declaration of Human Rights → United Nations General Assembly. All 193 member states of the UN have ratified at least one of the nine binding treaties influenced by the Declaration, with the vast majority ratifying four or more.
Who among these four was born earliest?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four. Osler created the first residency program for specialty training of physicians.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these four was born earliest?
George Grove (born 1820) is the earliest of the four. Grove was trained as a civil engineer, and successful in that profession, but his love of music drew him into musical administration.
Which of these four began earliest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Fritz Zwicky is an astronomer. Fritz Zwicky (German: [ˈtsvɪki]; February 14, 1898 – February 8, 1974) was a Swiss astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Ruthenium?
Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
What is the atomic number of Chlorine?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
In what year was Ernest Lawrence born?
Ernest Lawrence: A graduate of the University of South Dakota and University of Minnesota, Lawrence obtained a PhD in physics at Yale in 1925.
In what year was Richard Feynman born?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Klaus Schwab born?
Klaus Schwab: Klaus Martin Schwab (German: [klaʊs ˈmaʁtiːn ʃvaːp]; born 30 March 1938) is a German mechanical engineer, economist, and founder of the World Economic Forum (WEF).
In what year did Saint Valentine die?
Saint Valentine was a clergyman – either a priest or a bishop – in the Roman Empire who ministered to persecuted Christians.
In what year did Niels Bohr die?
Niels Bohr: Although the Bohr model has been supplanted by other models, its underlying principles remain valid.
In what year was Benzene discovered?
Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Perl: Larry Wall. Perl is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language.
IAI Kfir: Israel Aerospace Industries Ltd.
Which country is Beriev A-50 from?
Beriev A-50: Russia. Developed to replace the Tupolev Tu-126 "Moss", the A-50 first flew in 1978.
Who is credited with discovering Penicillin?
Penicillin: Alexander Fleming. Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
2C-B: Alexander Shulgin. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.
Who is credited with discovering Chromium?
Chromium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
When a message is designed to spark an immediate purchase, it's called the 'direct-response' kind of this consumer-facing practice. What is it?
Advertising is the practice and techniques employed to bring attention to a product or service.
Its type species, a common freshwater organism constantly studied in classrooms and labs, lends its name to an entire genus of shape-changing single-celled organisms — what's the genus?
Amoeba (genus) is a genus of single-celled amoeboids in the family Amoebidae.

This superfamily of tailless Old World primates, native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia and more closely related to Old World monkeys than New World ones, includes humans among its members — what's this group called?
Ape (hominoids), are a superfamily of Old World simians native to sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia.
These large Old World monkeys come in six distinct species, each native to a different region of Africa, with one species also found on the Arabian Peninsula — what primate is it?
Baboon are primates comprising the genus Papio, one of the 23 genera of Old World monkeys, in the family Cercopithecidae.
From molecules and cells up to whole ecosystems, this science studies living things through ideas like heredity, evolution, and homeostasis — what is it?
Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms.
This rhythmic bodily process draws oxygen-rich air into the lungs and expels carbon dioxide, powering the cellular chemistry that turns food into energy — what process is it?
Breathing (respiring or ventilating) is the rhythmic process of inhaling air into the lungs providing oxygen, and exhaling the air removing carbon dioxide, in the gas exchange process.
Indigenous to Asia, this genus of flowering plants includes species like sativa, indica, and ruderalis, and is also commonly known as hemp when grown for non-drug purposes — name the genus?
Cannabis is a genus of flowering plants in the family Cannabaceae that is widely accepted as being indigenous to and originating from the continent of Asia.

The only living member of its genus, this big cat sprints at up to 104 km/h thanks to powerful hindlimbs, long legs, and a flexible spine, and wears black tear-like streaks down its face; which animal is it?
Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is a species of large feline and the only living member of the genus Acinonyx.
Mostly belonging to the genus Naja, these venomous snakes are known for rearing upward and flaring a distinctive hood when threatened — name this common snake type?
Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja.
Tolerant of poor, sandy soil, this legume was domesticated in Africa millennia ago and is now grown far more in Nigeria and Niger than anywhere else on Earth — which crop?
Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.

First patented in Germany in 1920, then independently synthesized by an American chemist in 1932 and marketed in German-speaking Europe as Permonid for its fast onset and short duration, what is this semi-synthetic opioid?
Desomorphine (or in some formulations known as Krokodil) is a semi-synthetic opioid commercialized by Roche, with powerful, fast-acting effects, such as sedation and analgesia.
This soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida is also known by slang names like 'dew-worm,' 'rainworm,' and 'nightcrawler.' What creature is it?
Earthworm is a soil-dwelling terrestrial invertebrate that belongs to the phylum Annelida.
Comprising around 50 species mostly found in the tropics, this fungal genus infects rye, wheat, barley, and other grasses, producing toxic alkaloids — name the group of fungi?
Ergot is a group of fungi of the genus Claviceps. The most prominent member of this group is Claviceps purpurea (rye ergot fungus).
The excessive buildup of collagen-rich connective tissue after chronic inflammation or repeated injury, leaving a permanent scar that can choke off organ function — what's this process called?
Fibrosis is the development of fibrous connective tissue in response to an injury.

This computer scientist demonstrated a working prototype of his operating system CP/M in 1974 and later founded Digital Research — his invention of the BIOS helped make the personal computer revolution possible. Who is he?
Gary Kildall (May 19, 1942 - July 11, 1994) was an American computer scientist and microcomputer entrepreneur.

Five species of this group of plants — rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane — together cover 46 percent of the world's arable land, alongside two related families, sedges and rushes. What kind of plant is this?
Grass refers to various families of plants.
Which 19th-century American economist's wildly popular treatise Progress and Poverty argued that a single tax on the value of land could build a more just and productive society?
Henry George (September 2, 1839 - October 29, 1897) was an American political economist, social philosopher and journalist.
A body-temperature emergency defined as a reading above 104°F, this condition kills roughly half a million people annually and is most commonly triggered by heat stroke — what is it called?
Hyperthermia is a condition in which an individual's body temperature is elevated beyond normal due to failed thermoregulation.
This medical condition describes a restricted blood supply to tissue or an organ, starving cells of the oxygen they need and often resulting from a blocked or narrowed vessel — what is it called?
Ischemia is a restriction in blood supply to any tissue, muscle group, or organ of the body.
This Confederate veteran and pharmacist sold the rights to his 1886 beverage recipe to Asa Griggs Candler for about $2,300 shortly before he died — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton (July 8, 1831 - August 16, 1888) was an American pharmacist, chemist, and Confederate States Army officer who is best known as the inventor of Coca-Cola.
Endemic to New Zealand, this large, nocturnal, ground-dwelling parrot has owl-like forward-facing eyes and holds the title of the world's only flightless parrot — what bird is it?
Kākāpō (Mori:; pl.: kkp; Strigops habroptilus), sometimes known as the owl-parrot, is a species of large, nocturnal, ground-dwelling parrot of the superfamily Strigopoidea.
Popular in aquariums but a destructive invader in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, this venomous Indo-Pacific creature warns predators off with bold red and black stripes — what is it?
Lionfish (genus Pterois) are venomous marine fish native to the Indo-Pacific.
Domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte, this grain was grown by Native Americans alongside beans and squash in the 'Three Sisters' method — name the tall grass crop?
Maize (Zea mays), also known as corn, is a tall stout grass that produces cereal grain.
Driven by hormones, this coordinated pair of bodily rhythms — one governing the ovaries, the other the uterine lining — usually runs 21 to 35 days and begins around age 12. What is it called?
Menstrual cycle is a series of natural changes in hormone production and the structures of the uterus and ovaries of the female reproductive system that makes pregnancy possible.
Named from a Greek word for lead because its ores were once confused with lead ore, this chemical element bears the symbol Mo and atomic number 42 — name the element?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.

What term, coined in the mid-19th century and often attributed to pathologist Rudolf Virchow, describes the premature death of cells in living tissue due to external injury or infection, as opposed to programmed cell death?
Necrosis (from Ancient Greek (nkrsis) 'death') is a form of cell injury which results in the premature death of cells in living tissue by autolysis.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
This herbaceous annual vine produces edible pods and comes in bush or climbing cultivars; global output hit 28 million tonnes in 2022, led by India. What legume species is it?
Phaseolus vulgaris is a herbaceous annual plant. Its botanical classification, along with other Phaseolus species, is as a member of the legume family, Fabaceae.

This medical condition occurs when air collects in the space between the lung and chest wall, typically causing sudden, sharp one-sided chest pain and shortness of breath — what's the condition called?
Pneumothorax is collection of air in the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall.
Originating in Central Asia despite widespread cultivation elsewhere, this is the most commonly grown species of a fuzzy-skinned stone fruit — what is its scientific name?
Prunus armeniaca is the most commonly cultivated apricot species.
Physicists denote this stretching of light's wavelength — caused by relative motion, gravity, or cosmic expansion — with the symbol z; its opposite is called blueshift. What is it?
Redshift is an increase in the wavelength, or equivalently, a decrease in the frequency, of electromagnetic radiation (such as light).

Grown mainly from Eastern and Northern Europe into Russia, this cold-tolerant grain crop is a member of the wheat tribe and its vigorous growth suppresses weeds while providing early forage for animals — name it?
Rye (Secale cereale) is a grass grown extensively as a grain, a cover crop and a forage crop.
This Soviet rocket engineer led the early development of his country's space program and designed the R-7, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile — who is he?
Sergei Korolev was Soviet aerospace engineer (1907–1966).

Born in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents and raised by her mother after her father's death, this Princeton grad became the third woman on the U.S. Supreme Court after Barack Obama's 2009 appointment — name this justice?
Sonia Sotomayor (born June 25, 1954) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This small nocturnal marsupial sails between trees on membranes stretched from wrist to ankle, and its Latin name translates as 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps) is a small, omnivorous, arboreal, and nocturnal gliding possum.

This family of marine and freshwater fish can inflate themselves dramatically, revealing thin spines that stay hidden against their skin until they puff up — unlike their spinier, porcupine-like relatives — name this fish family?
Tetraodontidae is a family of marine and freshwater fish in the order Tetraodontiformes.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.
Native only to the wetlands of the Carolinas, which carnivorous plant snaps shut a 'jaw' formed from the tips of its leaves when an insect trips it?
Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States.
This noble gas, found in trace amounts in Earth's atmosphere, powers arc lamps, serves as a rare anesthetic, and was the first of its family coaxed into a genuine chemical compound — which element?
Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Unearthed in Montana by Jack Horner's team in 1987, this 20-foot horned dinosaur sported a bony neck-frill and lived roughly 75 million years ago — which species?
Achelousaurus: Genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from North America.
Often called the father of theoretical computer science, this Englishman gave us a famous 'machine' that formalized the very idea of computation — who was he?

Nicknamed 'lazy eye,' this childhood vision disorder occurs when the brain favors one eye over the other, and correcting the underlying cause doesn't restore sight right away — what is this condition?
Amblyopia: Failure of the brain to process input from one eye.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.
Known commonly as palms, this family of over 2,600 flowering plant species includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms mostly found in the tropics — what's the family called?
Arecaceae: Palm family of flowering plants.

Despite its name being something of a misnomer, this herding dog breed was developed in California and takes its name from imported collies that arrived alongside sheep from Down Under — what breed is it?
Australian Shepherd: American breed of dog. The Australian Shepherd, also known as the Aussie, is a breed of herding dog from the United States.
Making up nearly 40% of all known insects with around 400,000 described species, this order is distinguished by front wings hardened into protective cases called elytra — what creatures are these?
Beetle: Order of insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae; species widely consumed include mealworms and rhinoceros beetle larvae.
This small Old World flycatcher breeds in rocky habitats from the British Isles to Morocco and central China, staying put in milder areas but migrating from colder ones — what bird is it?
Black redstart: Species of bird. The black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine bird in the Old World flycatcher family.
Formed from the C5-T1 spinal nerve roots, this network of nerves runs through the neck and over the first rib to supply the shoulder, arm, and hand — what is it?
Brachial plexus: Network of nerves. This plexus extends from the spinal cord, through the cervicoaxillary canal in the neck, over the first rib, and into the armpit.
Developed in 1964 at Britain's Royal Radar Establishment and influenced by JOVIAL, this programming language was chosen by the UK Ministry of Defence in 1971 for military applications — what is it?
CORAL: Early programming language. The R was originally for "radar", not "real-time".
Derived from Greek words for 'heart' and 'study,' this branch of internal medicine covers coronary artery disease, heart failure, and electrophysiology — which medical field?
Cardiology: Branch of medicine dealing with the heart.
Triggered by anything from a stroke to a bout of altitude sickness, this dangerous buildup of fluid inside the skull raises pressure on brain tissue and can cause seizures or worse — what is it?
Cerebral edema: Excess accumulation of fluid in the brain.
This class of jawed fish — including sharks, rays, skates, and ghost-like chimaeras — has skeletons made entirely of cartilage rather than bone — what is it called?
Chondrichthyes: Class of jawed cartilaginous fish. Chondrichthyes are aquatic vertebrates with paired fins, paired nares, placoid scales, and conus arteriosus in the heart.
Recognizable by a prominent crest and curved bill, this Australasian parrot family includes 21 species, the smallest of which is the cockatiel — which family of birds?
Cockatoo: Any bird in the family Cacatuidae.
What is this — “Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body”?

Copulation (zoology): Animal sexual reproductive act in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body. In zoology, copulation is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
This medical sign turns the lips, nail beds, and ear lobes a bluish-purple hue when blood isn't carrying enough oxygen, and comes in central and peripheral forms — what is it called?
Cyanosis: Decreased oxygen in the blood. Cyanosis is apparent usually in the body tissues covered with thin skin, including the mucous membranes, lips, nail beds, and ear lobes.
Often called eczema, this term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness and rash — sometimes with tiny blisters, sometimes thickening over time. What is it?
Dermatitis: Inflammatory disease of the skin.

Developed in the early 1950s to replace the propeller-driven Skyraider, this US Navy carrier jet had a maximum takeoff weight of just 24,500 pounds — about half the Navy's specification — which aircraft?
Douglas A-4 Skyhawk: Carrier-based attack aircraft.

This Russian political scientist studies authoritarian governance and legislative process, taught at Moscow institutions for nearly a decade, and by 2022 had a YouTube channel with a million subscribers — who is she?
Dubbed 'the father of nuclear physics,' this New Zealander won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry despite proposing that atoms have a tiny, densely charged nucleus — who is he?
Ernest Rutherford: New Zealand physicist and chemist (1871–1937)
Beloved in gardens for gobbling up pests, this spiny mammal native to Iberia and Scandinavia was introduced to New Zealand in the late 1800s but is now Red Listed in Britain — what is it?
European hedgehog: Species of small spiny mammal.
Native to the Mediterranean and grown since ancient times, this teardrop-shaped fruit is technically a syconium and comes from the type species of a genus with over 800 members — what fruit is it?
Fig: Species of flowering plant, or its fruit.
This British-American theoretical physicist lent his name to a hypothetical genetically engineered 'tree' and a transform used in additive number theory — who was he?
Freeman Dyson: British theoretical physicist and mathematician (1923–2020)
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
This Russian-American engineer built the first successful four-engine aircraft in 1913 and went on to pioneer the modern helicopter — who was he?
Nicknamed 'Dr. Death,' this pathologist assisted at least 130 patients in dying and was convicted of murder after broadcasting one such case on television — who is he?
Jack Kevorkian: American pathologist and euthanasia activist (1928–2011)
The youngest division chief in GM history shepherded the Pontiac GTO before founding the motor company behind a stainless-steel sports car immortalized in Back to the Future — who was he?
John DeLorean: American automobile engineer and executive (1925–2005)
Sold under names like Toradol and Acular, this NSAID's use is capped at five days due to serious side-effect risk, with relief starting within an hour — what drug is it?
Described both as a science and as the art of justice, this set of enforced rules can be made by legislatures, executive decrees or judges' precedent — what is it?
A sweet, aromatic flavouring used in confectionery, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals comes from the root of which legume — though more than a couple of milligrams per kilo a day can cause trouble?
Often a complication of cancer treatment, this incurable, progressive swelling condition is managed with compression therapy and manual drainage rather than diuretics — what is it?
Lymphedema: Swelling due to a compromised lymphatic system.

The first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed as a university math professor, this Milanese scholar later traded calculus for four decades of theology and charity — who is she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi: Italian mathematician and philanthropist (1718–1799)
Triggered by falling progesterone, this regular discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred, and typically first arrives at menarche between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation: Periodic shedding of the uterine lining.
Nicknamed 'Foxbat' by NATO and built largely from stainless steel, this Soviet interceptor still holds the altitude record for an airbreathing piloted aircraft at 38 km — which jet?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Family of interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft.
Born in China and educated at MIT and Stanford, this billionaire engineer founded Taiwan's dominant chipmaker, serving as its CEO from 1987 to 2005 — who is he?
Morris Chang: Taiwanese businessman and electrical engineer (born 1931)

The males of this stocky Arctic cetacean sport a spiralled 'tusk' up to three metres long — actually a protruding left canine tooth thought to work as a weapon, a tool, and maybe a salinity sensor. What animal is it?
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American is regarded as the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines — who was he?
Norbert Wiener: American mathematician and philosopher (1894–1964)

Found above 3,500 metres on the Tibetan Plateau, this parasitic fungus grows out of moth larvae and is prized — despite containing arsenic — as an aphrodisiac in traditional Chinese medicine. What is it commonly called?
Ophiocordyceps sinensis: Species of fungus. It parasitizes larvae of ghost moths and produces a fruiting body which is valued in traditional Chinese medicine and Nepalese medicine as an aphrodisiac.
From a single western-Mediterranean flowering plant come both a notorious drug and the tiny dark seeds sprinkled on your bagel — which species is it?
Papaver somniferum: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family.

This term for 'parts in each thousand' is symbolized by ‰ — a percent sign with an extra zero — and sits right next to the percent sign in Unicode's General Punctuation block — what is this unit called?
Per mille: Unit for parts per thousand. The associated symbol is ‰, similar to a per cent sign % but with an extra zero in the divisor.

Also known as physiography, this branch of natural science studies the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere — as opposed to the branch focused on the built human environment. Which field of study?
Physical geography: Study of processes and patterns in the natural environment.
This large, structurally diverse family of plant compounds includes flavonoids and tannic acid, some of which were historically used as dyes and for tanning garments — what are they called?
Also called cherry laurel, this evergreen shrub native to the Black Sea region was once woven into wreaths for its resemblance to true bay laurel, though the two aren't closely related — which plant?
Prunus laurocerasus: Species of plant. It is not to be confused with its American relative Prunus caroliniana, which is also called cherry laurel.
The largest of the procyonid family, this North American mammal is famous for its facial mask, ringed tail, and remarkably dexterous front paws — which animal is it?
Raccoon: Medium-sized mammal native to North America.
Discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston and named for the rose color of one of its compounds, this rare silvery-white metal of the platinum group is used to enhance jewelry — which element?
Rhodium: Chemical element with atomic number 45 (Rh)
Extremely cold-hardy and thriving in poor soil, this cereal grass is a staple grain behind Scandinavian crispbread and a certain whiskey style — what is it?
Rye: Species of grain. Rye (Secale cereale) is a grass grown extensively as a grain, a cover crop and a forage crop.
A predatory arachnid with eight legs, grasping pincers and a stinger-tipped tail, this desert-loving hunter has a lineage going back some 430 million years to the Silurian — what is it?
Made up of the collarbone, the scapula, and the upper-arm bone meeting in a ball-and-socket joint, which body part lets the arm swing in a full circle?
Shoulder: Part of the body. The articulations between the bones of the shoulder make up the shoulder joints.
This frozen dessert blends ice with fruit juice or purée — and sometimes wine, liqueur, or honey — for a refreshing icy treat. What is it called?
Sorbet: Frozen dessert. Sorbet is a frozen dessert made using ice combined with fruit juice, fruit purée, or other ingredients, such as wine, liqueur, or honey.
Whose pure-white winter coat became 'ermine,' the prized fur trimming the ceremonial robes of the UK House of Lords — and which was disastrously introduced to New Zealand? What animal is it?
Sometimes called gadflies, the females of this fly family bite land animals, including humans, to get the blood protein they need to produce eggs — which family?
Tabanidae: Family of insects. Horse flies and deer flies are true flies in the family Tabanidae in the insect order Diptera.
Often called the oldest form of drama, this collaborative art puts live performers before a live audience, blending gesture, speech, song, music and dance in one place — what is it?
Theatre: Collaborative form of performing art. The performers may communicate this experience to the audience through combinations of gesture, speech, song, music, and dance.
Equal to exactly 1,000 kilograms — about 2,204.6 pounds — this unit of mass has an SI equivalent called the megagram. What is it called?

Tonne: Metric unit of mass equivalent to 1,000 kilograms or 1 megagram. It is also referred to as a metric ton in the United States to distinguish it from the non-metric units of the short ton and the long ton.
This reptile's defining feature is a shell developed mainly from its ribs, paired with a toothless, keratinized beak — what creature is it?
